origin_region: Sabaragamuwa Province · Ratnapura and Kegalle (sea level to 600 m)
cultivar: Assam-type seedling bushes and TRI clones
processing: Fully oxidised orthodox black tea in long leaf grades, similar to Ruhuna but from the wetter foothills of the Sinharaja and Adam's Peak ranges; smallholder green leaf processed by bought-leaf factories.
harvest_season: Year-round; a slight peak in quality in the first quarter.
appearance_dry: Long, black, well-twisted leaf, sometimes with reddish tips.
taste_profile: Full and smooth with sweet caramel and a hint of dark honey; a little softer and sweeter than Ruhuna, with less briskness than any hill tea.

brewing.notes: Four minutes, milk optional; takes a second steep.

vintage_note: Recognised by the Sri Lanka Tea Board as one of the island's seven tea districts; sold through the Colombo auction by factory and grade, almost entirely as low-grown leaf grades for the Middle East and CIS, and the district name rarely reaches a retail label. Buy the current year's lot and use within a year or two.
description:
Sabaragamuwa is the wet, low-lying province in the south-west of Sri Lanka around Ratnapura and Kegalle, on the foothills of the Sinharaja rainforest and Adam's Peak. The Sri Lanka Tea Board treats it as one of the island's seven tea districts, and in the cup it is the gentler sibling of Ruhuna: low-grown, dark and sweet, grown mostly by smallholders and made by bought-leaf factories.

The leaf grows fast in the heat and rain and is made into long, well-twisted orthodox leaf grades (OP, OP1, Pekoe, FBOP) with full oxidation; the factories aim for a black, handsome leaf and a thick, coloury liquor for the Middle Eastern and CIS markets.

The cup is dark coppery red, full and smooth with sweet caramel and a hint of dark honey, less briskness than any hill tea and a little more softness than Ruhuna. Boiling water, four minutes, milk optional; it will take a second steep.

It is sold through the Colombo auction by factory and grade, almost entirely as low-grown leaf grades, and the district name rarely reaches a retail label; most of it is sold as 'Ceylon OP' or 'low-grown Ceylon' or disappears into blends. Buy the current year's lot and use it within a year or two.

Worth a try if you want to understand what 'low-grown' means on a Ceylon label and why the Gulf prefers it.
